content: Thiomersal, also known as thimerosal in the United States, is an organomercury compound with the chemical formula C9H9HgNaO2S. It contains approximately 49% mercury by weight and has been used as an antiseptic and antifungal agent. This compound was developed and patented under the trade name Merthiolate in 1928 by the pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly and Company. Historically, thiomersal has been employed as a preservative in vaccines, immunoglobulin preparations, skin test antigens, antivenins, ophthalmic and nasal products, and even tattoo inks. In the United States, the European Union, and several other affluent countries, thiomersal has been phased out from vaccines routinely administered to children. This shift has been facilitated by the use of single-dose vaccine vials, which eliminate the need for bacteriostatic agents like thiomersal. However, thiomersal is still used in some formulations of inactivated influenza vaccines for children older than two years, as well as in certain vaccines not routinely recommended for young children, such as diphtheria-tetanus (DT), tetanus-diphtheria (Td), and tetanus toxoid (TT) vaccines. Additionally, trace amounts of thiomersal may remain in some vaccines due to manufacturing processes. Rarely used antivenins for pit viper, coral snake, and black widow venom also contain thiomersal. Outside North America and Europe, many vaccines still include thiomersal. The World Health Organization has stated that there is no evidence of toxicity from thiomersal in vaccines and no safety-related reason to switch to more expensive single-dose administration. Thiomersal is highly toxic when inhaled, ingested, or absorbed through the skin, with a risk of cumulative effects. It is also extremely toxic to aquatic organisms and may cause long-term adverse effects in aquatic environments. Within the human body, thiomersal is metabolized or degraded into ethylmercury (C2H5Hg+) and thiosalicylate. Animal studies suggest that thiomersal rapidly dissociates to release ethylmercury after injection. The mercury distribution patterns in the body are similar to those observed after exposure to equivalent doses of ethylmercury chloride. The central nervous system and kidneys are primary targets of toxicity, with impaired motor coordination being a common symptom. Similar signs and symptoms have been observed in cases of accidental human poisoning. The mechanisms underlying thiomersal's toxic effects remain unknown. Most of the compound is eliminated from the body through fecal excretion. Ethylmercury clears from the blood with a half-life of approximately 18 days and from the brain in about 14 days. However, inorganic mercury derived from ethylmercury has a much longer clearance time, at least 120 days. This form of mercury appears to be less toxic than inorganic mercury produced from mercury vapor, though the reasons for this difference are not well understood. Thiomersal has also been associated with allergic reactions. It is used in patch testing for individuals with dermatitis, conjunctivitis, and other potential allergic conditions. In some populations, such as in Germany, thiomersal sensitivity has been observed in a small percentage of individuals. For those sensitive to thiomersal, intramuscular immunization can be used instead of subcutaneous administration, making contact allergy clinically irrelevant in most cases. In Denmark, the prevalence of thiomersal allergy has decreased, likely due to its removal from vaccines. The potential link between thiomersal and autism has been a topic of significant controversy. Some parents, scientists, and doctors have suggested a connection between thiomersal exposure and autism. In the United States, numerous families have filed claims alleging that vaccines containing thiomersal caused autism in their children. However, the majority of these claims remain unresolved, and no awards have been granted. Despite the lack of convincing evidence supporting a causal relationship between thiomersal and autism, parental concerns about vaccines have contributed to a decline in childhood immunization rates and an increased risk of measles outbreaks. Thiomersal was first patented in 1927 by Morris S. Kharasch, a chemist at the University of Maryland, and the patent was granted to Eli Lilly in 1928. Early studies demonstrated that thiomersal was 40 to 50 times more effective than phenol against Staphylococcus aureus. It was widely used to kill bacteria and prevent contamination in antiseptic ointments, creams, jellies, and sprays, as well as in nasal sprays, eye drops, contact lens solutions, immunoglobulins, and vaccines. Thiomersal served as a preservative in multidose vaccine vials, which were more cost-effective than single-dose vials. By 1938, thiomersal was considered one of the most important drugs developed by Eli Lilly. Concerns about its safety first emerged in the 1970s when case reports suggested potential neurotoxicity when used in large volumes as a topical antiseptic. At that time, the diphtheria-pertussis-tetanus (DPT) vaccine was the only childhood vaccine containing thiomersal. A 1976 FDA review concluded that this use of thiomersal was not dangerous. In the 1990s, U.S. health authorities lowered reference doses for methylmercury, coinciding with a sharp rise in autism diagnoses. This led to concerns about thiomersal in vaccines, prompting its removal from most childhood vaccines by 2001. Some parents of autistic children attributed the increase in autism cases to thiomersal exposure and filed lawsuits against vaccine manufacturers. Despite scientific studies rejecting the mercury-autism hypothesis, it remains widely accepted among some parents of autistic children.
